Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{3}-9y$ that lies in the fourth quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-9y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-9) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=-3$ to $y=0.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-9y)=3{y}^{2}-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+(3{y}^{2}-9)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-3}^{0}({y}^{3}-9y)\sqrt{1+9({y}^{2}-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
